said-01-c1.text: British Red Cross. Unresponsive and breathing: learn first aid. British Red Cross.
said-01-c1.quote: When a person is unresponsive, their muscles relax and their tongue can block their airway so they can no longer breathe.
said-01-c1.claim: when a person is unresponsive, their muscles relax and their tongue can block their airway so they can no longer breathe

said-01-c1.text: Resuscitation Council UK. Defibrillation. Resuscitation Council UK.
said-01-c1.quote: For every minute that someone’s in cardiac arrest without receiving CPR and having a defibrillator used on them, their chance of survival decreases by 10%.
said-01-c1.claim: for every minute someone is in cardiac arrest without CPR and a defibrillator, their chance of survival falls by 10%

said-01-c1.text: Nobel Prize Outreach. Henry Dunant: Biographical. NobelPrize.org.
said-01-c1.quote: He arrived there in time to witness, and to participate in the aftermath of, one of the bloodiest battles of the nineteenth century.
said-01-c1.claim: arrived near the northern Italian town of Solferino in time to witness one of the bloodiest battles of the nineteenth century

said-01-c1.text: International Committee of the Red Cross (2016). History of the ICRC.
said-01-c1.quote: What was to become the International Committee of the Red Cross met for the first time in February 1863 in Geneva, Switzerland.
said-01-c1.claim: the committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross first met in Geneva in February 1863

said-01-c1.text: Museum of the Order of St John. James Cantlie: a key figure in the early history of St John Ambulance. Museum of the Order of St John.
said-01-c1.quote: When the St John Ambulance Association was established in 1877 to provide training in first aid, James became one of the Association’s first instructors.
said-01-c1.claim: the St John Ambulance Association was established in 1877 to provide training in first aid

said-01-c1.text: Hurt R (2005). Modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation: not so new after all. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine.
said-01-c1.quote: William Kouwenhoven (1886–1975) (Figure 5) rediscovered external cardiac compression by accident during his research on internal and external defibrillation, and so became the founder of modern CPR.
said-01-c1.claim: rediscovered external cardiac compression during his research on defibrillation

said-01-c1.text: Hurt R (2005). Modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation: not so new after all. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine.
said-01-c1.quote: This work culminated in 1960 when he reported a 70% survival rate in twenty patients and emphasized that it was possible to treat a cardiac arrest outside a hospital environment
said-01-c1.claim: In 1960 he reported a 70% survival rate in twenty patients

said-01-c2.text: Resuscitation Council UK. How to do CPR. Resuscitation Council UK.
said-01-c2.quote: 3 steps to save a life: check, call, CPR
said-01-c2.claim: Resuscitation Council UK boils the opening down to three steps: check, call, CPR

said-01-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to do the primary survey (DR ABCDE). St John Ambulance.
said-01-c2.quote: Kneel next to their chest and gently shake their shoulders, asking, ‘Are you OK?’, ‘Can you open your eyes?’.
said-01-c2.claim: Kneel by their chest, gently shake their shoulders

said-01-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to do the primary survey (DR ABCDE). St John Ambulance.
said-01-c2.quote: Treat life-threatening bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound before managing their airway
said-01-c2.claim: If blood is gushing or spurting, press on the wound before you deal with the airway

said-01-c2.text: Resuscitation Council UK. How to do CPR. Resuscitation Council UK.
said-01-c2.quote: Push down hard and then release twice per second, and don’t stop.
said-01-c2.claim: push down hard in the centre of the chest and release, twice per second, without stopping

said-01-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to do CPR. St John Ambulance.
said-01-c2.quote: If you are on your own do not leave the casualty to look for a defibrillator yourself.
said-01-c2.claim: if you are alone, do not leave the casualty to look for one

said-01-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). How to put someone in the recovery position. St John Ambulance.
said-01-c2.quote: If they remain in the recovery position for 30 minutes, roll them into the recovery position on the other side.
said-01-c2.claim: After 30 minutes, roll them onto the other side

said-01-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Hypothermia. St John Ambulance.
said-01-c2.quote: If you are in a remote area and cannot call for emergency help, send two people to get help together.
said-01-c2.claim: send two people for help together

said-01-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to do the primary survey (DR ABCDE). St John Ambulance.
said-01-c3.quote: During the first minutes of cardiac arrest, about half of casualties will do something called 'agonal gasping'.
said-01-c3.claim: about half of casualties do something called agonal gasping

said-01-c3.text: British Red Cross. Unresponsive and not breathing: learn first aid. British Red Cross.
said-01-c3.quote: Sometimes when a person is unresponsive their breathing may become noisy or irregular, or they may be gasping. This is usually a sign that their heart is not working properly and you should start chest compressions.
said-01-c3.claim: noisy, irregular or gasping breathing means start chest compressions

said-01-c3.text: British Red Cross. Unresponsive and not breathing: learn first aid. British Red Cross.
said-01-c3.quote: A damaged rib will mend, but if you don’t do chest compressions their chances of survival are much lower.
said-01-c3.claim: a damaged rib will mend, and without compressions their chances of survival are much lower

said-01-c3.text: British Red Cross. Unresponsive and not breathing: learn first aid. British Red Cross.
said-01-c3.quote: There’s no evidence to suggest you will cause any serious damage.
said-01-c3.claim: there is no evidence you will cause serious damage

said-01-c3.text: Resuscitation Council UK. FAQs: Basic Life Support. Resuscitation Council UK.
said-01-c3.quote: No such action has ever been brought against someone who performed CPR, and in general, the courts in the UK look favourably on those who go to the assistance of others.
said-01-c3.claim: no such action has ever been brought against someone who performed CPR

said-01-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to use a defibrillator (AED). St John Ambulance.
said-01-c3.quote: AEDs are built so that anyone, even without any training, can use them in an emergency.
said-01-c3.claim: AEDs are built so that anyone, even without any training, can use them in an emergency

said-01-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2026). How to use a defibrillator (AED). St John Ambulance.
said-01-c3.quote: For adults, place one AED pad on the upper right side of the chest, just beneath the collarbone, and the other on the lower left side, below the armpit.
said-01-c3.claim: one pad goes on the upper right side of the chest just beneath the collarbone and the other on the lower left side, below the armpit

said-02-c1.text: British Red Cross. First aid for someone bleeding heavily. British Red Cross.
said-02-c1.quote: You are acting as a “plug” to stop the blood escaping. The pressure you apply will help the blood clot and stop the bleeding.
said-02-c1.claim: you are acting as a plug to stop the blood escaping

said-02-c1.text: St John Ambulance (2026). Severe bleeding. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c1.quote: Shock is a life-threatening emergency, caused when the body doesn't have sufficient blood circulating to supply the vital organs with oxygen.
said-02-c1.claim: the body not having enough blood circulating to supply the vital organs with oxygen

said-02-c1.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c1.quote: A life-threatening bleed is extreme bleeding likely to cause death in minutes
said-02-c1.claim: extreme bleeding likely to cause death in minutes

said-02-c1.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c1.quote: Blood is quickly soaking through bandage after bandage
said-02-c1.claim: blood quickly soaking through bandage after bandage

said-02-c1.text: Maher D (2020). Innovations from the Battlefield: Tourniquets. Journal of Military and Veterans' Health.
said-02-c1.quote: rather was used by Hindu physicians in the 6th century BCE to treat Greek troops bitten by snakes unfamiliar to physicians.
said-02-c1.claim: Hindu physicians in the 6th century BCE used one to treat Greek troops bitten by snakes

said-02-c1.text: Lee C, Porter KM, Hodgetts TJ (2007). Tourniquet use in the civilian prehospital setting. Emergency Medicine Journal.
said-02-c1.quote: The first reported use of a tourniquet for haemorrhage control after wounding was by a French army surgeon called Etienne Morel in 1674.
said-02-c1.claim: a French army surgeon, Etienne Morel, in 1674

said-02-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2026). Severe bleeding. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c2.quote: Your priority is to stop the bleeding.
said-02-c2.claim: your priority is to stop the bleeding

said-02-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2026). Severe bleeding. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c2.quote: If the colour does not return within two seconds, the bandage is too tight.
said-02-c2.claim: If the colour has not come back within two seconds, the bandage is too tight

said-02-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c2.quote: Place the pad over the wound and hold tightly in place for a minimum of five minutes, in some instances the dressing may need to be packed tightly into the wound.
said-02-c2.claim: a haemostatic dressing is held tightly for at least five minutes and sometimes packed tightly into the wound

said-02-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c2.quote: Place the tourniquet around the limb close to and above the injury. If you can place it below the elbow or knee, this is best. It should never be placed on a joint.
said-02-c2.claim: a tourniquet goes close to and above the injury, never on a joint

said-02-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c2.quote: If you do not have a tourniquet, you can use items such as a triangular bandage, a scarf, or tie, and use a pen, a fork, or a Tourni-Key (if you have one) for the rod.
said-02-c2.claim: a triangular bandage, scarf or tie with a pen or fork as the rod, or a belt pulled tight

said-02-c2.text: British Red Cross. First aid for someone bleeding heavily. British Red Cross.
said-02-c2.quote: Don't wash a wound that is bleeding heavily. You may make it bleed more.
said-02-c2.claim: Do not wash a heavily bleeding wound

said-02-c2.text: British Red Cross. First aid for someone bleeding heavily. British Red Cross.
said-02-c2.quote: These kits are meant for anyone to use, even without training, to treat serious, life-threatening injuries.
said-02-c2.claim: Public bleed control kits, often kept beside defibrillators, are meant for anyone to use

said-02-c3.text: Maher D (2020). Innovations from the Battlefield: Tourniquets. Journal of Military and Veterans' Health.
said-02-c3.quote: Given these delays, the rudimentary surgical training, wound contamination and lack of antibiotics, limb amputation was frequent and would subsequently be attributed to the use of tourniquets.
said-02-c3.claim: the amputations were then blamed on tourniquets

said-02-c3.text: Lee C, Porter KM, Hodgetts TJ (2007). Tourniquet use in the civilian prehospital setting. Emergency Medicine Journal.
said-02-c3.quote: Lakstein identified that 5.5% of 110 pre‐hospital tourniquet applications resulted in neurological complications, with an ischaemic time between 109–187 min. None of these resulted in limb loss.
said-02-c3.claim: 5.5% caused nerve complications and none resulted in limb loss

said-02-c3.text: Maher D (2020). Innovations from the Battlefield: Tourniquets. Journal of Military and Veterans' Health.
said-02-c3.quote: during the Boston Marathon bombings, 27 tourniquets were applied, with no adverse outcomes reported.
said-02-c3.claim: 27 tourniquets were applied with no adverse outcomes reported

said-02-c3.text: Headquarters, Department of the Army (1992). FM 21-76: Survival. Internet Archive.
said-02-c3.quote: In a buddy system, however, the buddy can release the tourniquet pressure every 10 to 15 minutes for 1 or 2 minutes to let blood flow to the rest of the extremity.
said-02-c3.claim: said a buddy could release the pressure every 10 to 15 minutes for 1 or 2 minutes

said-02-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Life-threatening bleed. St John Ambulance.
said-02-c3.quote: Once a tourniquet is applied it should not be loosened as the bleeding will start again.
said-02-c3.claim: once a tourniquet is applied it should not be loosened, because the bleeding will start again

said-02-c3.text: Maher D (2020). Innovations from the Battlefield: Tourniquets. Journal of Military and Veterans' Health.
said-02-c3.quote: where a British medical manual, Injuries and Diseases of War, spectacularly criticised tourniquets

said-02-c3.text: Maher D (2020). Innovations from the Battlefield: Tourniquets. Journal of Military and Veterans' Health.
said-02-c3.quote: The US Army Institute of Surgical Research (2006) reported higher survival rates in patients with pre-hospital tourniquet use compared to hospital application (89% vs 78%).

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: Core temperature is tightly regulated with minimal diurnal variations at about 37 ± 0.5 °C.
said-03-c1.claim: Your core runs at about 37°C, held within half a degree

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: Involuntary shivering can counteract cooling by increasing the endogenous basal heat production up to 500% of baseline
said-03-c1.claim: shivering can raise your heat production to as much as five times normal

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: hypothermia can be the result of excessive transfer of energy to a cold environment through conduction, convection, evaporation, or radiation (primary hypothermia).
Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C (normal body temperature is around 37C).

said-03-c1.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2026). Preventing Hypothermia. CDC Winter Weather.
said-03-c1.quote: it can occur even at cool temperatures (above 40°F) if a person becomes chilled from rain, sweat, or submersion in cold water.
said-03-c1.claim: it can happen even above 40°F (about 4°C) if someone is chilled by rain, sweat or cold water

said-03-c1.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2026). Preventing Hypothermia. CDC Winter Weather.
said-03-c1.quote: This makes hypothermia especially dangerous, because a person may not know that it's happening and won't be able to do anything about it.
said-03-c1.claim: a person may not know it is happening and won't be able to do anything about it

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: Hypothermia I (mild) Conscious, shivering * 35–32 °C Hypothermia II (moderate) Impaired consciousness *; may or may not be shivering <32–28 °C

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: Accidental hypothermia has been recognised since ancient times
said-03-c1.claim: hypothermia has been recognised since ancient times

said-03-c1.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c1.quote: Throughout history, hypothermia has been a disease of war and disasters such as avalanches, earthquakes and tsunamis
said-03-c1.claim: a disease of war and of disasters such as avalanches and earthquakes

said-03-c1.text: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (2026). Heat-related Illnesses. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
said-03-c1.quote: When heat stroke occurs, the body temperature can rise to 106°F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes.
said-03-c1.claim: body temperature can rise to 106°F (41°C) or higher within 10 to 15 minutes

said-03-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Hypothermia. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c2.quote: Do not give them your clothes - it is important for you to stay warm yourself.
said-03-c2.claim: do not give them your own clothes: you need to stay warm too

said-03-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Hypothermia. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c2.quote: Lay them on a thick layer of dry insulating material, such as pine branches, heather, or bracken.
said-03-c2.claim: Lay them on a thick layer of dry insulation such as pine branches, heather or bracken

said-03-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Hypothermia. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c2.quote: If the casualty is fully alert, offer them warm drinks and high energy food such as chocolate.
said-03-c2.claim: If they are fully alert, warm drinks and high-energy food such as chocolate

said-03-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Frostbite. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c2.quote: Place the affected part into warm but not hot water – around 40°C.

said-03-c2.text: British Red Cross. Hypothermia: learn first aid. British Red Cross.
said-03-c2.quote: Don’t try to thaw the affected body part if there is any chance that it will refreeze
said-03-c2.claim: Do not thaw it if it could freeze again

said-03-c2.text: NHS. Heat exhaustion and heatstroke. NHS website.
said-03-c2.quote: They should start to cool down and feel better within 30 minutes.
said-03-c2.claim: They should feel better within 30 minutes

said-03-c2.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c2.quote: A patient who is unable to walk, should be placed in a horizontal position on a stretcher.
said-03-c2.claim: keep them lying flat if they cannot walk

said-03-c2.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c2.quote: rescue collapse may be coincidental during rescue, but is more likely to be caused by hypovolemia, cardiac dysrhythmias triggered by interventions, such as central venous catheterisation, biochemical changes, or, most frequently, by mechanical stimuli such as sudden movement
said-03-c2.claim: collapse during rescue is most often triggered by sudden movement

said-03-c2.quote: do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp to warm them up
said-03-c2.claim: No hot baths, hot water bottles or heat lamps

said-03-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Frostbite. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c3.quote: Do not rub the area as this could damage their skin.
said-03-c3.claim: St John Ambulance warns that rubbing could damage the skin

said-03-c3.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2026). Preventing Hypothermia. CDC Winter Weather.
said-03-c3.quote: Since skin may be numb, victims of frostbite can harm themselves further.
said-03-c3.claim: victims of frostbite can harm themselves further

said-03-c3.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Hypothermia. St John Ambulance.
said-03-c3.quote: Do not give the casualty alcohol in an attempt to warm them - it will make hypothermia worse.
said-03-c3.claim: St John Ambulance says alcohol will make hypothermia worse

said-03-c3.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2026). Preventing Hypothermia. CDC Winter Weather.
said-03-c3.quote: Know who is at high risk: older adults without proper food, clothing, or heating; people who stay outdoors for long periods (homeless, hikers, hunters, etc.); people who drink alcohol in excess or use illicit drugs
said-03-c3.claim: The CDC counts people who drink alcohol in excess among those at high risk of hypothermia

said-03-c3.text: NHS. Heat exhaustion and heatstroke. NHS website.
said-03-c3.quote: hot skin that's not sweating and might look red
said-03-c3.claim: The NHS lists hot skin without sweating among the signs

said-03-c3.text: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (2026). Heat-related Illnesses. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
said-03-c3.quote: Symptoms of heat stroke include: Confusion, altered mental status, slurred speech Loss of consciousness (coma) Hot, dry skin or profuse sweating
said-03-c3.claim: the CDC's list for heat stroke reads hot, dry skin or profuse sweating

said-03-c3.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c3.quote: In hypothermic patients, cardiac arrest may also be caused by afterdrop (further cooling, even after rewarming has started).
said-03-c3.claim: further cooling, even after rewarming has started

said-03-c3.text: Paal P, Pasquier M, Darocha T, Lechner R, Kosinski S, Wallner B, Zafren K, Brugger H (2022). Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.
said-03-c3.quote: The main cause of afterdrop is reperfusion of cold body parts during rewarming
said-03-c3.claim: mainly because blood starts flowing again through cold parts of the body

said-04-c1.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Burns and scalds. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c1.quote: The longer the burning goes on the more severe the injury.
said-04-c1.claim: the longer the burning goes on, the more severe the injury

said-04-c1.text: British Red Cross. First aid for burns. British Red Cross.
said-04-c1.quote: Cooling the burn is important because it will reduce pain, swelling and the risk of scarring.
said-04-c1.claim: it reduces pain, swelling and the risk of scarring

said-04-c1.text: British Red Cross. First aid for burns. British Red Cross.
said-04-c1.quote: The sooner and longer a burn is cooled with cold running water, the less the impact of the injury.
said-04-c1.claim: the sooner and longer a burn is cooled with running water, the less the impact

said-04-c1.text: World Health Organization (2026). Burns. WHO fact sheets.
said-04-c1.quote: In 2023, an estimated 163 000 people died worldwide from exposure to fire, heat and hot substances, according to WHO’s Global Health Estimates (GHE).
said-04-c1.claim: around 163 000 people died in 2023 from fire, heat and hot substances

said-04-c1.text: NHS. Sprains and strains. NHS website.
said-04-c1.quote: Torn or twisted ligament (tissue that connects the joints)
said-04-c1.claim: is a torn or twisted ligament, the tissue that connects the joints

said-04-c1.text: British Red Cross. First aid for a broken bone. British Red Cross.
said-04-c1.quote: The bone could be cracked, snapped, crushed or broken into a few pieces. No matter how the bone is broken, the first aid steps to help are the same.
said-04-c1.claim: whether it is cracked, snapped, crushed or in pieces, the first aid is the same

said-04-c1.text: Science Museum Group. Thomas splint. Science Museum Group Collection.
said-04-c1.quote: Invented in 1865 by Hugh Owen Thomas, a Welsh orthopaedic surgeon, the Thomas splint was designed to help immobilise fractures of the leg
said-04-c1.claim: invented in 1865 by the Welsh orthopaedic surgeon Hugh Owen Thomas

said-04-c1.text: Science Museum Group. Thomas splint. Science Museum Group Collection.
said-04-c1.quote: In December 1914, Thomas’ nephew Robert Jones was made Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon to the British Army.
said-04-c1.claim: made Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon to the British Army in December 1914

said-04-c1.text: Science Museum Group. Thomas splint. Science Museum Group Collection.
said-04-c1.quote: it wasn’t until 1917 that the splint was routinely supplied but as it was introduced progressively nearer to the battlefields it dramatically reduced both death rates and the degree of long-term disability.
said-04-c1.claim: once it was routinely supplied from 1917 it dramatically reduced death rates

said-04-c2.text: NHS. Burns and scalds. NHS website.
said-04-c2.quote: Hold the burn or scald under cool running water for 20 minutes. Do this as soon as possible, within 3 hours of it happening.
said-04-c2.claim: Hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible and within 3 hours

said-04-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Burns and scalds. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c2.quote: If there is no water available, you could use cold milk or canned drinks.

said-04-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Burns and scalds. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c2.quote: When the burn has cooled, cover the area loosely with cling film, lengthways.
said-04-c2.claim: with cling film laid along it, not wrapped round

said-04-c2.text: NHS. Sprains and strains. NHS website.
said-04-c2.quote: apply an ice pack (or a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a tea towel) to the injury for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.
said-04-c2.claim: protection, rest, ice wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, compression and elevation

said-04-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Broken bones and fractures. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c2.quote: Do this by holding the joint above and below the injured area.
said-04-c2.claim: support the limb by holding the joint above and below the injury

said-04-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). Broken bones and fractures. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c2.quote: You can secure an upper limb fracture with a sling and a lower limb fracture with broad fold bandages.
said-04-c2.claim: an arm in a sling, a leg with broad-fold bandages

said-04-c2.text: St John Ambulance (2025). How to make an arm sling. St John Ambulance.
said-04-c2.quote: Tie the two ends of the bandage together in a reef knot above their collar bone and tuck in the free ends.
said-04-c2.claim: tie a reef knot above the collarbone

said-04-c2.text: British Red Cross. First aid for a broken bone. British Red Cross.
said-04-c2.quote: Never attempt to put dislocations back in place as you may cause further damage.
said-04-c2.claim: push a joint back into place

said-04-c2.text: British Red Cross. First aid for burns. British Red Cross.
said-04-c2.quote: Avoid putting their whole body under a cold shower or in a cold bath as it could induce hypothermia.
said-04-c2.claim: a whole body in a cold bath or shower can bring on hypothermia

said-04-c3.text: British Red Cross. First aid for burns. British Red Cross.
said-04-c3.quote: Butter and cream contain oils. Oils retain heat, which is the opposite of what you’re trying to do.
said-04-c3.claim: butter and cream contain oils, and oils retain heat

said-04-c3.text: British Red Cross. First aid for burns. British Red Cross.
said-04-c3.quote: Toothpaste often contains menthol, which may give a superficial feeling of cooling, but does not effectively help a burn.
said-04-c3.claim: the menthol in toothpaste only gives a superficial feeling of cooling
